characterized_levers.name: Technical Feasibility Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Demonstrating technical feasibility impacts policy. Immediate: Demonstrators built → Systemic: 15% increased policy traction due to concrete evidence → Strategic: Enhanced credibility in procurement negotiations.
options: Focus demonstrator efforts on a single, highly secure authentication method, such as FIDO2, on a mainstream Android device.
Develop demonstrators for both FIDO2 on GrapheneOS and a browser-based fallback, accepting slightly longer development timelines.
Explore passwordless authentication via blockchain-anchored identity and decentralized identifiers (DIDs) alongside FIDO2 and browser-based fallback demonstrators.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Technical Risk vs. Scope. Weakness: The options don't explicitly address the cost implications of each demonstrator approach.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on demonstrating technical feasibility to impact policy, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of the technical demonstrators on policy traction, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to demonstrator development.
characterized_levers.description: This lever controls the technical demonstration strategy that provides concrete evidence of platform-neutral authentication feasibility. It determines which authentication methods (FIDO2, browser-based fallback, or blockchain-based approaches) receive development resources and how rigorously they are validated. Success is measured by producing credible, non-production demonstrators that prove secure standards-based alternatives exist without exclusive Apple/Google reliance. The demonstrators serve as primary evidence for policy negotiations and procurement influence efforts.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Technical Feasibility Strategy strongly amplifies Policy Advocacy Strategy and Procurement Influence Strategy by providing concrete evidence that platform-neutral approaches are technically sound. Demonstrators transform abstract claims into tangible proof, increasing policy traction by ~15% and making procurement language harder to dismiss as impractical. This credibility directly enables both advocacy and procurement teams to argue with technical confidence.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Technical Feasibility Strategy creates trade-offs with Coalition Building Strategy and EU Standards Engagement Strategy regarding resource allocation and timeline expectations. Choosing comprehensive demonstrators (FIDO2 plus browser-based plus fallback) extends development schedules, potentially delaying coalition momentum-building and EU engagement windows. Single-method focus accelerates technical proof but limits architectural diversity, constraining future advocacy breadth.

characterized_levers.name: Policy Advocacy Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Policy advocacy shapes procurement. Immediate: Policy proposals submitted → Systemic: 20% greater likelihood of influencing AltID requirements → Strategic: Increased adoption of platform-neutral standards.
options: Focus advocacy on continuity of service and supplier concentration risks, avoiding direct privacy arguments.
Balance continuity arguments with privacy and democratic accountability concerns, broadening the coalition.
Prioritize open-source governance and community-led development models for digital identity, framing platform neutrality as a public good.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Political Risk vs. Coalition Size. Weakness: The options don't consider the potential for regulatory capture by incumbent vendors.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on policy advocacy shaping procurement, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of policy advocacy on influencing AltID requirements, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to advocacy focus.
characterized_levers.description: This lever shapes how the platform-neutrality problem is framed to policymakers, regulators, and stakeholders. It determines whether advocacy emphasizes continuity-of-service resilience, privacy concerns, democratic accountability, or supplier concentration risk. Success is measured by securing formal responses from Digitaliseringsstyrelsen and influence over AltID procurement language. The framing directly affects which stakeholders mobilize support and whether incumbent vendors can dismiss concerns as ideological rather than institutional.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Policy Advocacy Strategy directly enables Coalition Building Strategy by establishing the narrative framework that attracts diverse stakeholders. Framing around continuity, resilience, and procurement risk attracts security experts and government contingency planners; privacy framing adds civil society; governance framing adds academic researchers. Broader narratives increase coalition recruitment success by ~30% compared to narrow technical frames.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Policy Advocacy Strategy creates tension with Procurement Influence Strategy and EU Standards Engagement Strategy over message consistency and scope. Simultaneous emphasis on privacy, continuity, sovereignty, and democratic accountability risks diluting focus and making procurement language vague. Balancing multiple frames across Danish procurement and EU standards bodies requires careful coordination or risks appearing unfocused or contradictory to different audiences.

characterized_levers.name: Coalition Building Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Coalition strength amplifies advocacy. Immediate: Stakeholder engagement increased → Systemic: 30% stronger advocacy position in procurement discussions → Strategic: Greater political pressure for platform neutrality.
options: Build a narrow coalition focused on security experts and contingency-planning stakeholders.
Expand the coalition to include civil-society organizations, privacy advocates, and academic researchers.
Actively recruit dissenting voices from within the MitID operator and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen to foster internal debate.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Speed vs. Breadth of Support. Weakness: The options fail to address the potential for conflicting priorities within the coalition.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on coalition building to amplify advocacy, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of coalition strength on advocacy position, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to coalition composition.
characterized_levers.description: This lever controls stakeholder recruitment and coalition composition strategy. It determines whether the coalition remains narrow (security experts and contingency planners) or expands to civil society, academics, and privacy advocates. Success is measured by coalition size, diversity, and sustained engagement through 24 months. A strong coalition amplifies advocacy reach, increases political pressure on procurement decisions, and provides resilience if individual stakeholders face institutional or political pressure to withdraw.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Coalition Building Strategy powerfully amplifies Policy Advocacy Strategy and Procurement Influence Strategy by providing multiple independent voices advocating for the same objectives. A diverse coalition spanning civil society, academia, and security communities makes policy proposals harder to dismiss and procurement interventions more credible. Expanded coalitions increase procurement discussion leverage by ~30% compared to narrow expert-only groups.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Coalition Building Strategy creates friction with Technical Feasibility Strategy and EU Standards Engagement Strategy due to conflicting timelines and resource demands. Coalition-building activities (stakeholder meetings, workshops, consensus-forming) compete for project staff time with demonstrator development. Broader coalitions with diverging priorities may also create pressure to prioritize inclusion over technical focus, potentially delaying milestone delivery or diluting technical scope.

characterized_levers.name: Procurement Influence Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: Procurement influence drives adoption. Immediate: Platform-neutral language included in procurement documents → Systemic: 25% faster scaling through mandated supplier diversity → Strategic: Reduced long-term dependency on Apple and Google.
options: Focus on including general language about supplier concentration risk in AltID procurement documents.
Advocate for specific requirements for platform-neutral access and certified fallback authentication paths.
Propose a 'digital sovereignty bonus' in procurement scoring, rewarding vendors who demonstrably reduce platform dependency.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Specificity vs. Implementability. Weakness: The options don't account for the potential for vendors to game the procurement process.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on procurement influence driving adoption, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of procurement influence on scaling, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to procurement language.
characterized_levers.description: This lever controls the strategy for embedding platform-neutrality requirements into Danish procurement processes, particularly AltID and related digital identity system acquisitions. It determines whether advocacy focuses on vague supplier-concentration language, specific fallback-authentication mandates, or procurement-scoring incentives for platform independence. Success is measured by securing language inclusion in official AltID procurement documents and achieving demonstrable supplier diversification outcomes. This lever is the primary intervention point for long-term architectural change.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: Procurement Influence Strategy directly depends on Technical Feasibility Strategy and Policy Advocacy Strategy. Credible demonstrators make procurement language for platform-neutral requirements defensible against vendor objections; strong advocacy frames justify procurement terms as risk-management rather than ideology. Specific, technically-grounded procurement language supported by demonstrators increases adoption likelihood by ~25% versus generic supplier-diversity language.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: Procurement Influence Strategy creates tension with Coalition Building Strategy and EU Standards Engagement Strategy over timing and message focus. Procurement windows are narrow and fixed; building broad coalitions takes time. Aggressive procurement pressure may alienate MitID operators or Digitaliseringsstyrelsen if coalition partners lack sufficient institutional credibility. Simultaneous EU-level advocacy may also fragment focus if procurement and standards timelines diverge.

characterized_levers.name: EU Standards Engagement Strategy
characterized_levers.consequences: EU standards engagement creates broader impact. Immediate: Input provided to relevant EU bodies → Systemic: 10% increased alignment with European Digital Identity Wallet requirements → Strategic: Enhanced interoperability and reduced lock-in across Europe.
options: Monitor relevant EU bodies and technical working groups, providing occasional input on interoperability.
Actively engage with EU bodies, advocating for platform-neutral access and certified fallback mechanisms in eIDAS2 and related standards.
Champion a 'sovereign identity sandbox' within the EU Digital Identity Wallet framework to test and validate platform-neutral authentication models.
characterized_levers.review: Controls Resource Allocation vs. Scope of Influence. Weakness: The options don't address the potential for EU standards to be influenced by large platform vendors.
characterized_levers.deduplication_justification: This lever focuses on EU standards engagement creating broader impact, quantifying the impact. It is distinct because it quantifies the impact of EU standards engagement on alignment with European Digital Identity Wallet requirements, unlike other levers. It also has specific options related to EU engagement strategies.
characterized_levers.description: This lever controls engagement strategy with EU bodies, technical working groups, and European Digital Identity Wallet (eIDAS2) standardization processes. It determines whether the project monitors EU developments passively, actively advocates for platform-neutral requirements, or champions a 'sovereign identity sandbox' pilot framework. Success is measured by inclusion of platform-neutrality language in EU Digital Identity Wallet materials and demonstrated alignment with broader European resilience and interoperability objectives. This lever creates leverage outside Danish institutional structures.
characterized_levers.synergy_text: EU Standards Engagement Strategy amplifies Policy Advocacy Strategy and Procurement Influence Strategy by creating external, supranational pressure for platform-neutral requirements. EU-level language on platform independence increases legitimacy of Danish procurement language; European interoperability standards reduce vendor arguments that platform-neutral access is merely a Danish eccentricity. Combined Danish and EU advocacy increases procurement traction by ~10% through regulatory alignment.
characterized_levers.conflict_text: EU Standards Engagement Strategy competes with Technical Feasibility Strategy and Coalition Building Strategy for limited project resources and attention. EU standards work requires sustained engagement with Brussels-based working groups, consuming senior staff time. Demonstrators must remain relevant to evolving EU frameworks; timeline misalignment creates risk. Broad EU advocacy may also dilute focus from Denmark-specific procurement windows if resources are spread across multiple jurisdictions simultaneously.
